name: Honey
summary: Broad-spectrum antibacterial and anti-biofilm wound dressing that also calms cough. A 2015 Cochrane review found honey dressings heal partial-thickness burns faster than conventional dressings; medical-grade products are FDA-cleared.
how: Apply medical-grade (gamma-irradiated) Manuka honey to clean wounds under sterile dressing, changed daily; thin layer on cooled minor burns. Sore throat: 1-2 tbsp raw honey or dissolved in warm water. Cough: 2.5 mL before bed (children over 1).
safety: Never give to infants under 12 months (botulism risk). Diabetics must count the sugar. Use medical-grade, not grocery honey, on serious wounds and consult a clinician. Raw honey carries pollen allergens.
origin: Appears in over 500 Ebers Papyrus remedies; Egyptian surgeons packed it into wounds after surgery.

name: Garlic
summary: Allicin-rich antimicrobial and cardiovascular herb. Meta-analyses show garlic supplements cut total cholesterol 10-12% and lower systolic blood pressure roughly 5-8 mmHg; it is also active against Giardia and other parasites.
how: Crush or chop raw garlic and rest 10-15 minutes to form allicin; eat 1-2 cloves daily. Aged garlic extract 600-1200 mg/day has the best cardiovascular data. For respiratory infections, crush into honey and take 1 tsp 2-3 times daily; dilute garlic oil for topical fungal use.
safety: Interacts with blood thinners (warfarin, aspirin) and HIV protease inhibitors; stop 7-10 days before surgery. Causes heartburn, GI upset and body odor; raw garlic held on skin causes contact dermatitis.
origin: Listed in 22 Ebers Papyrus remedies; pyramid workers received daily rations for strength.

name: Aloe Vera
summary: A 2007 meta-analysis in Burns found aloe healed first- and second-degree burns about 9 days faster than conventional care; trials also support psoriasis and radiation dermatitis.
how: Scoop the clear inner gel from a fresh leaf (avoid yellow latex) onto burns, sunburn or minor wounds, or use gel over 90% aloe. Internally, 1-3 oz daily of decolorized inner-fillet juice.
safety: Aloe latex is a harsh laxative causing cramping, diarrhea and electrolyte loss; long-term oral use of unprocessed aloe is possibly unsafe. Oral aloe interacts with diabetes drugs, digoxin, diuretics and laxatives. Avoid internally in pregnancy/breastfeeding. Whole-leaf extract with aloin is an IARC Group 2B possible carcinogen; topical use can cause dermatitis.
origin: Called the plant of immortality and left at tomb entrances; the Ebers Papyrus lists it for skin disease and burns.

name: Castor Oil
summary: Ricinoleic acid stimulates intestinal EP3 receptors, making castor oil an FDA-approved OTC laxative; it also has anti-inflammatory and wound-repair effects and is an emollient in modern dry-eye drops.
how: Constipation: 15-60 mL (1-4 tbsp) orally on an empty stomach, acting in 2-6 hours. Skin/hair: massage cold-pressed oil, thinned with coconut or jojoba oil. Joint pain: soak flannel in castor oil, place on the joint, cover with wrap and apply a warm compress.
safety: Never eat castor beans, which contain the lethal toxin ricin; only processed oil is safe. Oral use causes severe cramping, nausea and diarrhea, and long-term use brings electrolyte imbalance and dependence. May induce premature labor, so pregnant women should not take it orally without supervision.
origin: Ebers Papyrus staple for laxative, eye and ointment use; seeds found in tombs from 4000 BCE.

name: Frankincense
summary: Boswellic acids (notably AKBA) inhibit 5-lipoxygenase and leukotriene synthesis. Clinical trials show Boswellia extract meaningfully reduces knee osteoarthritis pain, and trials support benefit in Crohn's remission and asthma.
how: Standardized Boswellia serrata extract (30-65% boswellic acids), 300-500 mg two to three times daily with meals, since fat aids absorption. Diffuse the essential oil for respiratory and stress support or dilute 2-3% for inflamed joints; chew food-grade resin for oral health or steep it as tea.
safety: May interact with anti-inflammatory drugs, blood thinners and lipid-lowering medications. Can cause GI upset, reflux and nausea. Pregnant women should avoid concentrated supplements; never ingest undiluted essential oil, and always dilute for skin.
origin: Burned in temples ('to make divine'); Hatshepsut sent an expedition to Punt to obtain the trees.

name: Myrrh
summary: Sesquiterpene-rich resin with broad antimicrobial and oral-health activity; furanoeudesma-1,3-diene activates mu-opioid receptors, giving a molecular basis for its analgesic reputation, and a myrrh preparation proved effective against schistosomiasis.
how: Mouthwash: 5-10 drops of tincture in a glass of warm water, gargle and rinse. Tincture 1-2 mL (20-40 drops) in water 2-3 times daily for oral or throat infection. Apply 2-3% diluted essential oil or tincture to wounds, canker sores or gums; burn resin as a fumigant.
safety: Pregnant women must avoid it entirely: myrrh is a uterine stimulant and may cause miscarriage. Large oral doses irritate the kidneys and alter heart rate. It may lower blood sugar (diabetics monitor glucose) and can interact with anticoagulants; contact dermatitis is possible.
origin: Central to embalming and to Ebers Papyrus wound, mouth-rinse and pain remedies.

name: Black Cumin
aka: Nigella sativa, black seed, seed of blessing
summary: Thymoquinone-rich seed studied in over 1,000 papers. A 2017 meta-analysis found significant reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c, cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides, and a 2013 meta-analysis showed about 5 mmHg lower systolic blood pressure; trials also show asthma improvement.
how: Chew 1/2 to 1 tsp seeds daily or sprinkle on food; black seed oil 1-3 tsp (2.5-5 mL) daily, plain or in honey; capsules 200-500 mg of oil or extract 2-3 times daily. Apply the oil to eczema or acne, or as a hair treatment.
safety: Interacts with blood-thinning, blood pressure and diabetes medications (hypoglycemia risk); stop 2 weeks before surgery as it slows clotting. High doses may damage liver or kidneys. Pregnant women should stay at culinary amounts; start low to gauge tolerance.
origin: Found in Tutankhamun's tomb and prized as a remedy for 'everything except death'.

name: Blue Lotus
summary: Mildly psychoactive flower whose aporphine alkaloid nuciferine acts as a dopamine D2 antagonist with anxiolytic effects; trace apomorphine partly explains its aphrodisiac reputation. Evidence is largely preclinical.
how: Tea: steep 5-10 g dried flowers in hot water 10-15 minutes, one cup. Traditional wine infusion: soak flowers in wine for hours to days, which extracts alkaloids more effectively. Tinctures follow product dosing; smoking or vaporizing petals carries respiratory risk.
safety: Legal status varies by country, and unregulated products vary widely in potency. Do not combine with MAO inhibitors, sedatives or erectile-dysfunction drugs. May cause nausea at higher doses; do not drive or operate machinery. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
origin: Soaked in wine for religious ceremonies and banquets; linked to the sun god Ra and rebirth.

name: Coriander
summary: Seed rich in linalool with antimicrobial action against Salmonella, E. coli and Listeria; it raises digestive enzyme secretion, lowers blood glucose by enhancing insulin release, and reduces cholesterol and triglycerides while raising HDL.
how: Tea: steep 1-2 tsp crushed seeds in 1 cup boiling water for 10 minutes, drunk after meals. Use seeds and fresh leaves liberally in food. Tincture 1-2 mL in water three times daily; dilute the essential oil in carrier oil for sore muscles.
safety: Very safe in food amounts. May lower blood sugar, so diabetics should monitor glucose. Coriander/cilantro allergy occurs and cross-reacts with mugwort and birch pollen. Do not ingest undiluted essential oil; topical use may increase photosensitivity.
origin: Seeds found in Tutankhamun's tomb; used in the Ebers Papyrus for digestive and urinary complaints.

name: Juniper
summary: Terpinen-4-ol raises glomerular filtration for a genuine diuretic effect, and the oil is active against urinary pathogens including E. coli and Klebsiella, supporting traditional UTI use.
how: Tea: crush 1 tsp dried berries, steep 15 minutes, 1-2 cups daily short term. Dilute oil to 2% for sore joints; tincture 1-2 mL three times daily briefly.
safety: Do not use in pregnancy (uterine stimulant) or with kidney disease, as juniper irritates the kidneys. Limit to 4-6 weeks maximum. May interact with lithium and diabetes medications and may increase menstrual flow. Use only Juniperus communis, never toxic savin juniper (J. sabina).
origin: Ebers Papyrus remedy for digestion, urinary complaints and chest conditions; berries found in tombs.

name: Fenugreek
summary: 4-hydroxyisoleucine stimulates insulin secretion; a landmark trial found 25 g/day of seed powder cut fasting glucose 25% in type 2 diabetes. Trials also show increased breast-milk output and higher testosterone.
how: Soak 1-2 tsp seeds overnight, then drink the water and eat the seeds. Capsules 500-600 mg standardized extract 2-3 times daily with meals, or 1-2 tsp powder in food or warm milk.
safety: Causes uterine contractions, so avoid in pregnancy except possibly at term under supervision. Adds to the glucose-lowering effect of diabetes medications and interacts with blood thinners via coumarin content. Can trigger allergy in people reacting to peanuts, chickpeas or other legumes; causes maple-syrup body odor and GI bloating.
origin: Ebers Papyrus remedy for burns, labor and digestion; Egyptian women used it for milk supply and cramps.

name: Willow Bark
summary: Contains salicin, the compound the body converts to salicylic acid and the basis of aspirin. A 2001 Rheumatology trial found 240 mg/day salicin as effective as rofecoxib for low back pain, with additional trials in osteoarthritis.
how: Decoction: simmer 1-2 tsp dried bark in 1 cup water 10-15 minutes, up to 3 cups daily. Standardized extract supplying 120-240 mg salicin daily. Tincture 2-3 mL three times daily. Onset is slower than aspirin but the effect lasts longer.
safety: Do not give to anyone under 18 (Reye's syndrome risk) or to anyone allergic to aspirin or NSAIDs. Interacts with blood thinners, NSAIDs, beta-blockers and methotrexate. Avoid with peptic ulcers, bleeding disorders or kidney disease, and in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
origin: One of the most frequently cited analgesics in Egyptian texts; chewed for headache and used on swelling.

name: Pomegranate
summary: Punicalagin-rich juice cut carotid intima-media thickness 30% over a year in a 2004 trial; as complementary support in prostate cancer, juice slowed PSA doubling time from 15 to 54 months post-treatment. Root-bark pelletierine alkaloids paralyze tapeworms.
how: Drink 8 oz (240 mL) pure juice daily for cardiovascular benefit, or eat the arils regularly. Standardized extract 500-1000 mg daily. Gargle diluted juice or use pomegranate oral rinses for plaque and gum inflammation.
safety: Do not self-treat parasites with root-bark preparations, which are toxic at wrong doses. Juice has grapefruit-like CYP3A4 interactions with statins, ACE inhibitors and blood thinners, and may add to antihypertensive drugs. Juice is high in sugar and calories; extract may suit supplementation better.
origin: The Ebers Papyrus prescribed root bark specifically to expel tapeworms; fruit symbolized abundance.

name: Celery and Caraway
aka: Apium graveolens and Carum carvi seeds
summary: Celery seed's 3-n-butylphthalide lowers uric acid and eases gout and joint pain, and its apigenin is anxiolytic; caraway's carvone and limonene are antispasmodic and carminative, with a 2013 trial showing caraway oil helps functional dyspepsia.
how: Celery seed tea: steep 1 tsp crushed seeds 10 minutes, 1-2 cups daily; or standardized celery seed extract 75-150 mg twice daily for joints. Caraway tea: 1-2 tsp crushed seeds steeped 10 minutes after meals. Use both liberally in cooking.
safety: Celery causes photosensitivity from psoralens and common allergies, may interact with blood thinners and lithium, and concentrated seed supplements should be avoided in pregnancy. Caraway is very safe but may lower blood sugar; dilute its essential oil for topical use.
origin: Both appear in the Ebers Papyrus, celery seed for joint stiffness and urinary retention, caraway for colic.

name: Acacia Gum
summary: Gum arabic is a soluble prebiotic fiber that grows Bifidobacteria and Lactobacilli; a 2012 Kidney International study found it lowered CRP and oxidative stress in chronic kidney disease. Fermenting acacia gum makes lactic acid, which is spermicidal, explaining the ancient pessary.
how: Gum arabic powder 5-30 g dissolved in water daily as prebiotic fiber. Mixed with water it forms a soothing protective film for skin. The contraceptive use is historical only; modern methods are far more reliable.
safety: May reduce absorption of oral medications taken at the same time, so separate doses by 2 hours. Expect bloating and gas when starting fiber supplementation. Some people are allergic to acacia.
origin: The Ebers and Kahun Papyri describe acacia tips ground with honey and dates on a lint pessary as contraception.

name: Onion
summary: The richest dietary source of quercetin, which inhibits COX and lipoxygenase pathways; a 2015 meta-analysis found quercetin supplementation lowers systolic blood pressure 3-7 mmHg, and onion reduces platelet aggregation and feeds gut bacteria via fructans.
how: Eat raw or lightly cooked onions regularly. Cough syrup: slice an onion, layer with honey, let sit overnight and take 1 tbsp of the syrup as needed. Quercetin supplements 500-1000 mg/day for anti-inflammatory effect.
safety: Can cause heartburn and digestive discomfort and may interact with blood-thinning medications. Raw onion juice irritates skin and eyes. Onions are highly toxic to dogs and cats, so keep away from pets.
origin: Sacred symbol of eternity; the Ebers Papyrus prescribed onion for colds, parasites and heart disease.

name: Cumin
summary: Boosts pancreatic enzyme secretion and bile flow; a 2014 trial found cumin improved all IBS symptoms, a 2017 meta-analysis showed lower fasting glucose and HbA1c, and a trial found LDL down 10% and triglycerides down 23%.
how: Use generously in cooking. Tea: steep 1 tsp seeds in hot water 10 minutes, drunk after meals. Powder 1-3 g daily in food or water; 3 g/day reduced weight and BMI in one trial in overweight women.
safety: Very safe in food amounts. May lower blood sugar, so diabetics on medication should monitor. Large medicinal doses reduced male fertility in animal studies, and cumin may cause photosensitivity.
origin: Ebers Papyrus remedy for flatulence, colic and diarrhea; also used in food preservation and embalming.

name: Thyme
summary: Thymol is a powerful antiseptic, the active ingredient in Listerine since 1879. A 2006 study found thyme extract as effective as bromhexine for productive cough, and German Commission E approves thyme for bronchitis.
how: Tea: steep 1-2 tsp dried thyme in hot water 10 minutes, 2-3 cups daily for respiratory support. Cough syrup: infuse fresh thyme in honey 2 weeks, then take 1 tsp as needed. Diffuse the essential oil, or dilute 1-2% in carrier oil for antifungal use.
safety: Thyme essential oil is very potent: never apply undiluted or ingest it. May slow blood clotting, so avoid before surgery. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy (culinary amounts are safe). Can cause allergic reactions in people sensitive to the mint (Lamiaceae) family.
origin: Valued by Egyptians as an embalming preservative, and used for coughs, chest complaints and temple incense.
